Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Zimbabwe primarily use manual paper-based systems for recording criminal cases and complaints, relying on physical dockets prone to loss, tampering, and bribery. Academic studies (e.g., 2019 GIS crime mapping in rural Chivi district) describe traditional crime registers and dockets, with data collected via manual processes and GPS for analysis, indicating no routine digital entry at point of service. ZRP has centralized digital databases (e.g., Criminal Records Office), but rural stations forward paper dockets for processing. Plans for an electronic docket system ("soon" transition announced Dec 2025) and internet provision to rural stations (pledged 2021, per Horizon 2025) remain unimplemented, with no evidence of rural rollout or pilots shifting the norm. Key barriers: poor internet/electricity in rural areas, low device access, resource constraints, as noted in World Bank digital economy report and POTRAZ analyses. National ambitions (e.g., smart policing) contrast sharply with rural paper reality, where digital tools like DMR radios exist for comms but not case recording. Score 1 reflects entirely paper-based point-of-service recording.

revision_notes: Confirmed. December 2025 reporting shows the Zimbabwe Republic Police still describing the transition to an electronic docket system as forthcoming ("soon"), announced by a Harare Province commissioner as future work, with no evidence of an implemented rural station-level digital case-recording system. revised_comments: Rural police stations in Zimbabwe continue to rely on manual paper-based dockets and registers for recording criminal cases and complaints at the point of service. As of December 2025, the Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) publicly describes a planned transition to an electronic docket management system as still forthcoming ("soon"), confirming that station-level digital case recording has not yet been implemented nationally, let alone in rural areas. A 2021 government pledge to provide internet connectivity to rural police stations to support digitisation remains largely unrealised. Poor rural internet and electricity access, combined with limited device availability, continue to constrain digital adoption at rural stations, while centralised systems such as the Criminal Investigations Department's Interpol-linked databases operate independently of rural point-of-service recording.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Zimbabwe rely entirely on paper-based processes for birth registration, requiring parents to present physical documents such as national ID cards, birth confirmation records (from hospitals/clinics), marriage certificates, baptismal certificates, witness IDs, or letters from village heads/farmers for home/farm births. No evidence found of electronic recording at the point of service in rural facilities; processes emphasize manual declarations and forms. Registration completeness is low in rural areas (~32% in 2015 vs higher urban), with rural residence a key predictor of non-registration alongside poverty, home births, and low maternal education Comparative Population Studies. Nationally, moderate digitization (50-64%) exists for aggregation, but rural point-of-service remains paper due to infrastructure gaps, limited staffing, and indirect costs like transport to district offices UNECA CRVS Report. Recent national digital initiatives (e.g., ZPR integration with health for automated notifications, planned 2023) focus on central systems, starting urban, with mobile apps piloted but no rural rollout confirmed; rural lags persist Biometric Update. Barriers: poor connectivity, economic crisis, under-resourced offices. Gap: National ambitions for e-CRVS contrast with rural paper reality, where data likely transcribed later at district level.

revision_notes: Confirmed. As of July 2025, digital ID/population registry issuance under the reformed Zimbabwe Population Registry System (ZPRS) is starting only in Harare and Bulawayo, with rural extension still pending. Rural registration activity in 2025 (e.g. the Binga mobile registration drive) uses temporary mobile teams to reach remote communities rather than a permanent rural digital registry office system. Rural registry offices remain paper/manual at point of service. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) is supported.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Zimbabwe continue to depend on paper-based processes at the point of service, requiring parents and applicants to present physical documents including national identity cards, hospital birth confirmation records, marriage certificates, witness statements, or letters from village heads or farmers for home or farm births. As of mid-2025, the reformed Zimbabwe Population Registry System, which underpins the government's planned digital ID rollout, is being introduced only in Harare and Bulawayo, with extension to the rest of the country not yet under way. Mobile registration drives in remote districts such as Binga rely on temporary outreach teams rather than digitised rural registry offices. National birth registration completeness stood at 57% in the 2023-24 Zimbabwe Demographic and Health Survey, with rural residence remaining a significant predictor of non-registration. Persistent barriers include poor connectivity, under-resourced offices, and the cost and distance involved in reaching district registration centres.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Zimbabwe primarily use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Data is collected via annual school census forms filled manually at schools and aggregated upward to the national EMIS, often leading to delays, gaps, and inaccuracies due to manual transcription at district levels. Most rural schools lack digital devices, internet connectivity, and power, preventing real-time digital entry into EMIS; teachers in areas like Mutoko report no access to digital tools for data contribution.Kuyenda Collective EMIS exists nationally, with high continental compliance scores and plans for decentralization, but rural point-of-service remains analog.UNESCO IICBA Pilots like school management software or e-learning platforms (e.g., Ruzivo) target urban/private schools or supplementary use, not routine admin recording in rural public primaries. Key barriers: poor infrastructure (no electricity/internet), teacher ICT skills gaps, funding shortages, high attrition. National policies (e.g., Education 5.0) aspire to digital inclusion, but rural reality lags far behind, with data digitized only post-collection at higher levels. (148 words)

revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2025 ED46 school census form, used to collect data from primary schools including rural ones, still asks schools to report whether they hold "digitalised school records (Management Information System)" as a yes/no item, confirming this is not yet universal. A 2026 UNICEF/MoPSE procurement for a new web-based school registration information management system indicates that a proper digital data-capture platform for schools, including satellite/rural tracking, is still in development rather than deployed. revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Zimbabwe continue to rely on paper-based registers and forms for recording administrative data, attendance and learning outcomes at the point of service. The Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education's annual ED46 school census, most recently updated for 2025, still asks schools to declare whether they maintain digitalised school records, indicating that digital data capture is not standard practice, particularly in under-resourced rural schools lacking computers, electricity and internet connectivity. Plans to merge the Teacher Development Information System with the national Education Management Information System (EMIS) and to decentralise data capture remain in progress rather than realised, and a new school registration information management system commissioned in 2026 is still under development. Rural schools such as those in Mutoko district report no access to digital tools for administrative data entry, with information gathered on paper and transcribed at higher administrative levels.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zimbabwe traditionally rely on paper registers for patient data recording, with aggregate data later entered into national DHIS2 at district levels. The Impilo EMR system, developed since 2015, is now deployed in 1,254 of ~1,900 public health facilities (66%), explicitly targeting rural 'last mile' sites like Sipepa Rural Hospital through solar power (1,044 facilities, 60% coverage) and internet upgrades to enable digital point-of-care recording. Provincial data (Matabeleland South, Q1 2025) shows 72% fully functional among 153 facilities, though rural districts lag. Digital systems are the emerging standard at most facilities, reducing paper burden and improving patient management, but some paper persists in the remaining ~34% uncovered sites and where infrastructure fails. Key barriers include frequent power outages (costing 6% GDP), poor rural internet/connectivity, training gaps, and staff shortages. National eHealth Strategy (2021-2025) bridges policy ambition with rollout, though rural implementation trails urban areas; majority now predominantly digital with residual paper processes.

revision_notes: Confirmed. As of August 2025, 1,254 of Zimbabwe's approximately 1,900 public health facilities (66%) are implementing the Impilo Electronic Health Records system, with further expansion planned. Provincial data from Matabeleland South (a largely rural province, Q1-Q2 2025) show 90.2% of facilities with EHR infrastructure installed, though only 71.9% fully functional, with rural districts (Bulilima, Matobo) disproportionately affected by power and connectivity gaps; comparable results are reported for Manicaland (88% coverage, 68% functional). This supports "Mostly digital - some paper" (3) rather than "Entirely digital" (4), given the persistent functional and rural coverage gaps. Score of 3 is confirmed and not promoted to the top of the scale.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zimbabwe are now substantially digitised at the point of care through the Impilo Electronic Health Records system, though paper-based processes persist alongside digital records in a meaningful minority of facilities. As of August 2025, 1,254 of approximately 1,900 public health facilities nationally, around two-thirds, have Impilo deployed, with further expansion under way. Provincial data from the largely rural Matabeleland South province (Q1-Q2 2025) show 90.2% of facilities with EHR infrastructure installed, though only 71.9% fully functional, with rural districts such as Bulilima and Matobo disproportionately affected by unreliable electricity and connectivity; similar patterns are reported in Manicaland province. Zimbabwe's National eHealth Strategy (2021-2025) and continued donor support, including the Global Fund's Digital Health Impact Accelerator, are extending solar power, internet connectivity and digital diagnostic systems to "last mile" rural facilities such as Sipepa Rural Hospital, but frequent power outages, poor rural connectivity and training gaps mean a residual share of rural clinics still rely on paper records.
